Adlm.name: Adlam
Adlm.source_note: glyphs original; right-to-left direction and optional joining shared with Arabic

Afak.name: Afaka
Afak.source_note: unrelated to any other script; acrophonic rebus; devised 1908; still taught as grade-1 Afaka among the few literate in it

Aghb.name: Caucasian Albanian
Aghb.source_note: attributed by tradition to Mashtots; arrangement close to Armenian; Greek the model for both

Ahom.name: Ahom, Tai Ahom
Ahom.source_note: brought at the conquest c. early 13th c., apparently on a Mon example; no dated early object; religious use into the 19th c.; modern use from a 1920 dictionary

Arab.name: Arabic
Arab.source: Hoyland, 'The birth of Arabic in stone'; Robin et al. 2014, CRAI
Arab.source_note: earliest dated text in Arabic script Zabad, 512; Namara (328) and Jabal Ramm are in Nabataean script

Armi.name: Imperial Aramaic
Armi.source_note: first attested in inscriptions of the 9th-8th c. BCE; distinct from Phoenician by the mid-8th c.

Armn.name: Armenian
Armn.source_note: arranged in Greek order; derivation of the letter shapes from Greek, Iranian or Aramaic still argued

Avst.name: Avestan
Avst.source: Unicode ch.10; Hoffmann, Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Avestan script'
Avst.source_note: created about the 5th-6th c. CE for the Avesta; earliest manuscript 1288; still used in Zoroastrian liturgy

Bali.name: Balinese
Bali.source_note: from Kawi; Belanjong pillar 914, Old Balinese beside Sanskrit

Bamu.name: Bamum
Bamu.source_note: Arabic via Hausa traders is the most cited stimulus; European and Vai models also proposed

Bass.name: Bassa Vah
Bass.source_note: may have been influenced by Vai; typeset from 1907

Batk.name: Batak
Batk.source_note: no proto-forms found; a manuscript in the British Library by 1764; introduction date unknown

Beng.name: Bengali (Bangla)
Beng.source_note: Gaudi (proto-Bengali) current from the 10th to the 14th c.; a distinct Bengali from the 14th-15th c.

Berf.name: Beria Erfe
Berf.source_note: devised in the 1950s by Adam Tajir from livestock brand marks; revised 2004; left to right

Bhks.name: Bhaiksuki
Bhks.source_note: used 10th-13th c.; eleven inscriptions and four manuscripts known

Blis.name: Blissymbols
Blis.source_note: an ideographic system inspired by Chinese characters, devised 1942-1949

Bopo.name: Bopomofo
Bopo.source_note: adopted 1913 from simplified Han forms (Zhang Binglin), promulgated 1918

Brah.name: Brahmi
Brah.source: Bright 1996, in Daniels & Bright; Salomon 1998, Indian Epigraphy
Brah.source_note: Aramaic origin after Buhler is the majority view; not settled; earliest securely dated texts the Ashokan edicts, c.250 BCE

Brai.name: Braille
Brai.source_note: a six-dot recoding of the French Latin alphabet, after Barbier's twelve-dot phonetic code

Bugi.name: Buginese
Bugi.source_note: of the Brahmic type and perhaps related to Javanese

Buhd.name: Buhid
Buhd.source: Unicode ch.17; Miller, Unicode Technical Note 35
Buhd.source_note: related to Tagalog but may not descend from it; within the range of 17th-c. Philippine handwriting

Cakm.name: Chakma
Cakm.source_note: Brahmic, an early offshoot of the Mon-Burmese script; no dated early manuscript found

Cans.name: Unified Canadian Aboriginal Syllabics
Cans.source_note: most characters drawn from British shorthand; Evans knew Devanagari, but no source makes it his model

Cari.name: Carian
Cari.source_note: a development parallel to, and independent of, Greek cannot be ruled out

Cham.name: Cham
Cham.source_note: Old Cham at Dong Yen Chau, c.4th c., in Pallava script

Cher.name: Cherokee
Cher.source_note: Sequoyah took letter shapes from Latin print without their Latin values, 1815-1821

Chis.name: Chisoi
Chis.source_note: invented in 1986 by Jayanta Kumar Mahata from Kurmali ritual and rangoli signs

Chrs.name: Chorasmian
Chrs.source_note: from Imperial Aramaic; dated cursive from Toprak-Kala, 3rd c. CE; earlier dates in the proposal unresolved

Cirt.name: Cirth
Cirt.source_note: a runiform script built by Tolkien on the model of Germanic runes

Copt.name: Coptic
Copt.source_note: Old Coptic papyri of the 1st-2nd c. CE; Greek letters plus six or seven from Demotic

Cpmn.name: Cypro-Minoan
Cpmn.source_note: Enkomi tablet of Late Cypriot I, c.1525-1475 BCE; derived from Linear A by sign form

Cprt.name: Cypriot syllabary
Cprt.source_note: the Palaepaphos obelos (11th c. BCE) may be the last Cypro-Minoan text rather than the first Cypriot one

Cyrl.name: Cyrillic
Cyrl.source: Slavica Occitania 12 (2001), after the Kirilo-Metodievska enciklopedija
Cyrl.source_note: earliest epigraphy Krepcha 921, a Preslav sherd 931, a dated Dobrudja inscription 943

Deva.name: Devanagari (Nagari)
Deva.source_note: no authentic specimen before the Silahara inscriptions at Kanheri, 851 and 877-878

Diak.name: Dives Akuru
Diak.source_note: descended from Brahmi through Grantha; closest to medieval Sinhala

Dogr.name: Dogra
Dogr.source: Pandey, L2/15-234; Unicode ch.15; Indian Express 2026
Dogr.source_note: Dogra written from the 17th c.; standardised in the 1860s; no longer used actively, Dogri now in Devanagari; signboard revival begun in Jammu, 2026

Dsrt.name: Deseret (Mormon)
Dsrt.source_note: Pitman's phonotypy the starting point, then an entirely new set of characters, adopted Dec 1853; not actively promoted after 1869; now of interest to historians and hobbyists

Dupl.name: Duployan shorthand, Duployan stenography
Dupl.source_note: a geometric shorthand, letterforms from circles and lines, for writing French

Egyd.name: Egyptian demotic
Egyd.source: Depauw, A Companion to Demotic Studies
Egyd.source_note: develops out of late hieratic in the 7th c. BCE; the earliest named object is not sourced here

Egyh.name: Egyptian hieratic
Egyh.source: Regulski, Oxford Handbook of Topics in Archaeology
Egyh.source_note: earliest hieratic on the stone vessels under the Step Pyramid, late 2nd dynasty to Djoser

Egyp.name: Egyptian hieroglyphs
Egyp.source: Baines 2004, in Houston (ed.), The First Writing
Egyp.source_note: independent Egyptian invention is the majority view; stimulus from Sumer is argued and not excluded

Elba.name: Elbasan
Elba.source_note: a Greek flavour to some characters, most letters new creations

Elym.name: Elymaic
Elym.source_note: derives from Aramaic; earliest on coins of the 2nd c. BCE

Ethi.name: Ethiopic (Geʻez)
Ethi.source: Drewes, RIE III/B; Breton 2019, Cahiers d'etudes africaines
Ethi.source_note: earliest Ge'ez text the Addi Gelemo sceptre, late 2nd to early 3rd c. CE; vocalised under Ezana

Gara.name: Garay
Gara.source: Everson, Unicode N4709; Pandey, Unicode N4044
Gara.source_note: influences of the Arabic writing system; written right to left
Gara.glyph_miss: no Noto face published (tried NotoSansGaray, NotoSerifGaray, NotoGaray)

Geok.name: Khutsuri (Asomtavruli and Nuskhuri)
Geok.source_note: Greek provenance most widely accepted; Aramaic shapes argued; earliest inscriptions dated 430s, some earlier claims

Geor.name: Georgian (Mkhedruli and Mtavruli)
Geor.source_note: first Mkhedruli inscription at Ateni Sioni, 982-986

Glag.name: Glagolitic
Glag.source_note: the search for the formal origins of Glagolitic remains unsolved

Gong.name: Gunjala Gondi
Gong.source_note: not genetically related to other scripts, but strongly resembles Modi; c.1750 is a researchers' claim, 1942 the firm evidence

Gonm.name: Masaram Gondi
Gonm.source_note: no genetic relationship to other writing systems, but based upon the Brahmi model

Goth.name: Gothic
Goth.source: Schaffner 2024, Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics
Goth.source_note: Wulfila's alphabet on the Greek model, with Latin and runic letters, c.350; manuscripts 5th-6th c.

Gran.name: Grantha
Gran.source_note: Pallava is the ancestor of Grantha; Grantha itself designed around 600 CE

Grek.name: Greek
Grek.source: Janko, on Methone; Jeffery, Local Scripts of Archaic Greece
Grek.source_note: Dipylon jug c.740 BCE and Nestor's cup; Gabii c.770 on the traditional chronology; earliest texts right to left

Gujr.name: Gujarati
Gujr.source_note: closely related to Devanagari; texts wholly in Gujarati from the late 15th c.; 1592 unsourced

Gukh.name: Gurung Khema
Gukh.source_note: an alphasyllabary based upon the Brahmi model, created 1995
Gukh.glyph_miss: no Noto face published (tried NotoSansGurungKhema, NotoSerifGurungKhema, NotoGurungKhema)

Guru.name: Gurmukhi
Guru.source: Pandey, L2/10-011; Mann 1996, The Goindval Pothis
Guru.source_note: Landa the model; the Goindval Pothis of the 1570s are the earliest extant source; 1539 was a guruship date

Hanb.name: Han with Bopomofo (alias for Han + Bopomofo)
Hanb.name_fr: han avec bopomofo (alias pour han + bopomofo)

Hang.name: Hangul (Hangŭl, Hangeul)
Hang.source_note: five or six consonant shapes from Phags-pa (Ledyard); the Haerye derives them from the speech organs

Hano.name: Hanunoo (Hanunóo)
Hano.source: Unicode ch.17; Miller, Unicode Technical Note 35
Hano.source_note: related to Tagalog but may not descend from it; within the range of 17th-c. Philippine handwriting

Hatr.name: Hatran
Hatr.source_note: inscriptions from 98-97 BCE to about 241 CE

Hebr.name: Hebrew
Hebr.source_note: the square Hebrew script grew out of Imperial Aramaic; Mount Gerizim inscriptions 3rd-2nd c. BCE

Hira.name: Hiragana
Hira.source: Unicode ch.18; Seeley 1991, A History of Writing in Japan
Hira.source_note: a 9th-c. development from cursive man'yogana; no securely dated first object

Hluw.name: Anatolian Hieroglyphs (Luwian Hieroglyphs, Hittite Hieroglyphs)
Hluw.source: van den Hout 2020, A History of Hittite Literacy, ch.7
Hluw.source_note: Egyptian inspiration unlikely; probably an Anatolian creation from indigenous signs

Hmng.name: Pahawh Hmong
Hmng.source: Unicode ch.16; Smalley, Vang & Yang 1990, Mother of Writing
Hmng.source_note: devised by Shong Lue Yang in 1959; some letters may recall Lao and Latin

Hmnp.name: Nyiakeng Puachue Hmong
Hmnp.source_note: several consonant letters appear derived from Hebrew characters; 1980s

Hntl.name: Han (Traditional variant) with Latin (alias for Hant + Latn)
Hntl.name_fr: han (variante traditionnelle) avec latin (alias pour Hant + Latn)

Hung.name: Old Hungarian (Hungarian Runic)
Hung.source: Everson & Szelp, Unicode N3483; Demeczky et al., Unicode N4371
Hung.source_note: thought to derive ultimately from Old Turkic; some treat them as distant relatives only

Inds.name: Indus (Harappan)
Inds.source: Farmer, Sproat & Witzel 2004, EJVS 11-2; Rao et al. 2009, Science 324
Inds.source_note: whether the signs encode language at all is disputed

Ital.name: Old Italic (Etruscan, Oscan, etc.)
Ital.source_note: from the Euboean Greek of Ischia and Cumae; Marsiliana abecedary 7th c. BCE; mostly right to left

Jamo.name: Jamo (alias for Jamo subset of Hangul)
Jamo.name_fr: jamo (alias pour le sous-ensemble jamo du hangûl)

Java.name: Javanese
Java.source_note: Kawi is the ancestor of Javanese and Balinese

Jurc.name: Jurchen
Jurc.source_note: many characters copies or distorted copies of Chinese and Khitan large script

Kali.name: Kayah Li
Kali.source_note: ordering and some shapes show Brahmic relation, most shapes developed independently

Kana.name: Katakana
Kana.source_note: Todaiji fujumonko, 824-834, the earliest katakana used for an extended Japanese text

Kawi.name: Kawi
Kawi.source: de Casparis 1975, Indonesian Palaeography; Pandey, L2/12-125
Kawi.source_note: Plumpungan c.750; de Casparis doubts direct descent from Pallava

Khar.name: Kharoshthi
Khar.source_note: no securely dated document before the Ashokan edicts at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra, mid-3rd c. BCE

Khmr.name: Khmer
Khmr.source_note: earliest dated Old Khmer K.557/600, 611; close to the Pallava script of the Coromandel coast
Khmr.native: អក្សរខ្មែរ

Khoj.name: Khojki
Khoj.source_note: a refined form of the Lohanaki variety of Landa, in use by the 16th c.; primers still published in Pakistan; used in Nizari Ismaili ceremonies

Kitl.name: Khitan large script
Kitl.source: Kane 2009, The Kitan Language and Script
Kitl.source_note: on the basis of Chinese clerical script with modifications; most characters novel

Kits.name: Khitan small script
Kits.source_note: created after contact with Uighurs; phonetic components, no shared characters with the large script

Knda.name: Kannada
Knda.source_note: Halmidi inscription, mid-5th c., in Kadamba script; a sister of Telugu

Kpel.name: Kpelle
Kpel.source_note: devised in the 1930s by Gbili; stimulated by the syllabic organisation of Vai

Krai.name: Kirat Rai
Krai.source_note: derived from the Old Kirat script from which Limbu also comes; Sumhung Lipi of the 1920s, redesigned 2000
Krai.glyph_miss: no Noto face published (tried NotoSansKiratRai, NotoSerifKiratRai, NotoKiratRai)

Kthi.name: Kaithi
Kthi.source_note: Kaithi and Devanagari are siblings within the Nagari family

Lana.name: Tai Tham (Lanna)
Lana.source_note: developed from the Mon script of Hariphunchai; earliest evidence 1376
Lana.native: อักษรธรรมล้านนา

Laoo.name: Lao
Laoo.source: Lorrillard, 'Scripts and history: the case of Laos'
Laoo.source_note: Fakkham the prototype of Lao script; no direct Khmer transmission; first dated stele 1494 or 1497

Latn.name: Latin
Latn.source: Rocca & Sarullo 2007; CNR 2011 on the Praeneste fibula; Gippert 2020
Latn.source_note: Lapis Niger and Lapis Satricanus 6th c. BCE; the Praeneste fibula (7th c.) is still argued over

Leke.name: Leke
Leke.source_note: created mid-19th c. with the Leke religion; some borrowing from Old Mon and Burmese

Lepc.name: Lepcha (Róng)
Lepc.source_note: based directly on Tibetan; invented around 1720

Limb.name: Limbu
Limb.source_note: oldest known writings collected in Darjeeling in the 1850s; 18th-c. Sirijanga origin is tradition

Lina.name: Linear A
Lina.source_note: Linear A grew out of the Cretan hieroglyphic tradition, which has no ISO code

Linb.name: Linear B
Linb.source: Olivier 2012, in Cline (ed.), Oxford Handbook of the Bronze Age Aegean
Linb.source_note: Knossos tablets 14th c. BCE on the compromise chronology; 1450 is the high date

Lisu.name: Lisu (Fraser)
Lisu.source_note: Sara Ba Thaw and James Fraser modified the shapes of Latin letters, 1908-1914, published 1915

Loma.name: Loma
Loma.source_note: devised in the 1930s by Wido Zobo; Vai stimulus, no shared letterforms

Lyci.name: Lycian
Lyci.source_note: both the letter shapes and the chronology point to a Greek origin; c.500 BCE

Lydi.name: Lydian
Lydi.source_note: Greek or Phrygian model, an open question; late 8th or early 7th c. BCE; mostly right to left

Mahj.name: Mahajani
Mahj.source_note: often called a derivative of Kaithi or Devanagari; structure resembles Landa

Maka.name: Makasar
Maka.source_note: closest relative Rejang; no evolutionary relationship with Buginese

Mand.name: Mandaic, Mandaean
Mand.source_note: based on the script of the Elymaean rock inscriptions; Unicode also allows Parthian chancery; bowls 4th-7th c.

Mani.name: Manichaean
Mani.source: Unicode ch.10; Everson, Unicode N2544 and N3486
Mani.source_note: based on Estrangela Syriac and Palmyrene; also described as a sister of Syriac out of Aramaic

Marc.name: Marchen
Marc.source_note: quite different from Tibetan and Lantsa; no early texts known, likely a much more recent innovation; widely used in modern Bon literature and inscriptions

Medf.name: Medefaidrin (Oberi Okaime, Oberi Ɔkaimɛ)
Medf.source_note: strong influence of English orthography, capital and small letters; revealed 1927

Mend.name: Mende Kikakui
Mend.source_note: syllabic blueprint unquestionably influenced by Vai; right to left

Merc.name: Meroitic Cursive
Merc.source: Rilly, UCLA Encyclopedia of Egyptology; Priese 1973
Merc.source_note: developed from Demotic; earliest datable object a sistrum handle naming Arnekhamani, c.220 BCE

Mero.name: Meroitic Hieroglyphs
Mero.source_note: created under Taneyidamani, first half of the 2nd c. BCE, from Egyptian hieroglyphs with new values

Mlym.name: Malayalam
Mlym.source_note: the 830 Vazhappalli plates are in Vatteluttu; Malayalam script texts from about the 12th c.

Modi.name: Modi, Moḍī
Modi.source: Pandey, Unicode N4034; Salomon 1998 n.116; Unicode ch.15; Hindustan Times 2025
Modi.source_note: a Nagari-family script for continuous writing; earliest extant document early 17th c.; formally discontinued in the 1950s; taught again for reading archives

Mong.name: Mongolian
Mong.source_note: adopted 1204 by tradition; earliest surviving text the Stele of Yisungge, c.1224-1225

Moon.name: Moon (Moon code, Moon script, Moon type)
Moon.source: Everson, Unicode N4128 (L2/11-280); Perkins School for the Blind
Moon.source_note: embossed symbols simplified from Latin letters; developed by William Moon in 1845

Mroo.name: Mro, Mru
Mroo.source_note: a messianic script of the 1980s with no genetic relationship to existing scripts

Mtei.name: Meitei Mayek (Meithei, Meetei)
Mtei.source_note: earliest use dated 11th-12th c., from the Tibetan group; Tomba 1993 calls the old documents forgeries

Mult.name: Multani
Mult.source_note: related to Gurmukhi; used in the 19th and 20th c.; earlier date unsourced

Mymr.name: Myanmar (Burmese)
Mymr.source_note: first inscription 11th c. (Myazedi c.1113); Mon source in Unicode, Pyu argued by Aung-Thwin
Mymr.native: မွန်မြန်မာအက္ခရာ

Nagm.name: Nag Mundari
Nagm.source_note: organisation modelled on Ol Chiki; developed from the 1950s

Nand.name: Nandinagari
Nand.source_note: a sister of Devanagari within the Nagari family, 11th c.

Narb.name: Old North Arabian (Ancient North Arabian)
Narb.source: Al-Jallad 2015, An Outline of the Grammar of the Safaitic Inscriptions; Unicode ch.10
Narb.source_note: shares an ancestor with Ancient South Arabian rather than descending from it

Nbat.name: Nabataean
Nbat.source_note: Elusa inscription early 2nd c. BCE not yet Nabataean in form; Aslah inscription, Petra, 95 BCE

Newa.name: Newa, Newar, Newari, Nepāla lipi
Newa.source_note: a distinct Newar script from the 10th c.; Lankavatara Sutra manuscript dated 908

Nkdb.name: Naxi Dongba (na²¹ɕi³³ to³³ba²¹, Nakhi Tomba)
Nkdb.source: Poupard 2019, Written Language & Literacy; Yang & He 2024
Nkdb.source_note: earliest dated manuscripts 13th c.; independence hedged, created amid Chinese and Tibetan literacy

Nkgb.name: Naxi Geba (na²¹ɕi³³ gʌ²¹ba²¹, 'Na-'Khi ²Ggŏ-¹baw, Nakhi Geba)
Nkgb.source_note: some characters from Dongba, some from Yi, Tibetan and Chinese; a dated stele of 1619

Nkoo.name: N’Ko
Nkoo.source: Unicode ch.19; Oyler 2005; Wyrod 2019, African Studies Review
Nkoo.source_note: Kante tried Arabic ajami and Latin before devising N'Ko in 1949; direction and joining as Arabic

Nshu.name: Nüshu
Nshu.source: UNESCO 2018; Endo, Unicode N4626; UNESCO Courier 2018; Unicode ch.18
Nshu.source_note: no securely dated object before the 19th c.; claims of a Song origin have no object behind them; very few fluent writers left by the late 20th c.; revived by local and national authorities

Ogam.name: Ogham
Ogam.source_note: the most likely immediate source is Latin; Greek and runes have had adherents

Olck.name: Ol Chiki (Ol Cemet’, Ol, Santali)
Olck.source_note: alphabetic, sharing none of the syllabic properties of Indic scripts; shapes from familiar objects

Onao.name: Ol Onal
Onao.source_note: invented by Mahendra Nath Sardar between 1981 and 1992; Bhumij was written in Odia, Bengali, Devanagari and Latin
Onao.glyph_miss: no Noto face published (tried NotoSansOlOnal, NotoSerifOlOnal, NotoOlOnal)

Orkh.name: Old Turkic, Orkhon Runic
Orkh.source: Everson et al., L2/08-071R2; Shcherbak 1996, Etudes mongoles 27
Orkh.source_note: Aramaic via Iranian scripts is mainstream; a direct Sogdian link is denied by Rona-Tas

Orya.name: Oriya (Odia)
Orya.source_note: early Oriya texts in Gaudi (Urajam 1051); a distinct Oriya script from the 14th c., of composite origin

Osge.name: Osage
Osge.source_note: letters in origin modifications or fusions of Latin letters, designed by 2006, revised 2012-2014

Osma.name: Osmanya
Osma.source: Unicode ch.19; Tosco, AAP, after Cerulli 1932
Osma.source_note: letter order follows Arabic; Latin gave only the direction; no Ethiopic role

Ougr.name: Old Uyghur
Ougr.source_note: believed to derive from Sogdian cursive in the 8th or 9th c.

Palm.name: Palmyrene
Palm.source_note: inscriptions from 44 BCE to about 280 CE

Pauc.name: Pau Cin Hau
Pauc.source_note: no genetic relationship with any other writing system; revealed 1902, alphabetic form 1931

Pelm.name: Proto-Elamite
Pelm.source: Dahl 2005, CDLJ 2005:3; Englund, Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Elam iii'
Pelm.source_note: unquestionably inspired by proto-cuneiform; numerical systems borrowed, signs largely new

Perm.name: Old Permic
Perm.source_note: modelled on Greek and Cyrillic, with many glyphs taken from tamga signs

Phag.name: Phags-pa
Phag.source_note: devised for Khubilai and promulgated in 1269; similar to Tibetan

Phli.name: Inscriptional Pahlavi
Phli.source_note: Sasanian inscriptions from 224 CE; descent through the Persis coin script is denied by Rezakhani

Phlp.name: Psalter Pahlavi
Phlp.source_note: 6th or 7th c. CE, after 552; more archaic than Book Pahlavi

Phlv.name: Book Pahlavi
Phlv.source_note: earliest dated witnesses the Elephantine papyri, 619-629 CE; the 4th-c. sarcophagus anchor is Islamic-period

Phnx.name: Phoenician
Phnx.source_note: first long text the Ahiram sarcophagus, c.1000 BCE on palaeography; its date is disputed

Plrd.name: Miao (Pollard)
Plrd.source_note: structure adopted from Cree syllabics, with Latin, shorthand and Miao signs

Piqd.name: Klingon (KLI pIqaD)
Piqd.source_note: built on ten characters designed for Star Trek: The Motion Picture, 1979

Prti.name: Inscriptional Parthian
Prti.source: Skjaervo, Encyclopaedia Iranica 'Iran vi.3'; MacKenzie, 'Dates and dating'
Prti.source_note: Nisa ostraca of the 1st c. BCE, one dated 89 BCE

Psin.name: Proto-Sinaitic
Psin.source_note: most scholars agree it derives from Egyptian hieroglyphs; first attested 19th c. BCE (Wadi el-Hol)

Ranj.name: Ranjana
Ranj.source_note: developed from the Newar (pacumola) model; first in Nepal in 1099

Rjng.name: Rejang (Redjang, Kaganga)
Rjng.source_note: first attested about the mid-18th c.

Rohg.name: Hanifi Rohingya
Rohg.source_note: influenced by Arabic but a modern construction with no direct genetic affiliation; finalised 1980

Roro.name: Rongorongo
Roro.source: Ferrara et al. 2024, Scientific Reports 14:2794; Wieczorek et al. 2021, J. Island & Coastal Arch.
Roro.source_note: first recorded 1864 (Eyraud); stimulus from the 1770 Spanish annexation treaty is argued and unresolved

Runr.name: Runic
Runr.source_note: thought to come from North Italic; Vimose comb c.150-160; written in either direction

Samr.name: Samaritan
Samr.source: Barag, in Cambridge History of Judaism; Langlois 2019
Samr.source_note: a conscious creation of the 4th c. CE; Cross and Purvis argued a Hasmonean branch of paleo-Hebrew

Sara.name: Sarati
Sara.source: Everson, Unicode N4013; Smith 2007, Parma Eldalamberon
Sara.source_note: Tolkien's first Elvish script, from 1919; the precursor of Tengwar

Sarb.name: Old South Arabian
Sarb.source: Hasselbach, in The Semitic Languages; Sass
Sarb.source_note: split off a Proto-Canaanite variant before 1000 BCE; Sass derives it from Phoenician-type letters

Saur.name: Saurashtra
Saur.source_note: Brahmic, exact derivation unknown; Randle 1943 records it printed in 1880

Sgnw.name: SignWriting
Sgnw.source_note: developed in 1974 by Valerie Sutton out of her DanceWriting

Shaw.name: Shavian (Shaw)
Shaw.source: University of Reading, Kingsley Read alphabet collection
Shaw.source_note: a 48-character alphabet for English, shapes new, 1960

Shrd.name: Sharada, Śāradā
Shrd.source_note: descended from Gupta through Kutila; Proto-Sarada from the 7th c., Sharada of Kashmir from the 8th

Shui.name: Shuishu
Shui.source_note: about half the characters derive from Chinese in mirrored or inverted form

Sidd.name: Siddham, Siddhaṃ, Siddhamātṛkā
Sidd.source_note: evolved out of the Gupta script in the late 6th c.; Bodh-Gaya inscription of Mahanaman, 588-589

Sidt.name: Sidetic
Sidt.source_note: origins not clearly known; thought to develop from Phoenician in parallel with Greek

Sind.name: Khudawadi, Sindhi
Sind.source_note: a Landa-based script related to Sharada; standard form published 1868; now obsolete; Bible Society printing continued past 1900

Sinh.name: Sinhala
Sinh.source_note: Brahmi inscriptions of the 3rd-2nd c. BCE; later influenced by Grantha

Sogd.name: Sogdian
Sogd.source_note: derived from Old Sogdian, used from the 7th to the 14th c. CE

Sogo.name: Old Sogdian
Sogo.source_note: Ancient Letters securely dated 312-313 CE; the Kultobe inscriptions possibly earlier

Sora.name: Sora Sompeng
Sora.source_note: of the Brahmic type, consonants with an inherent vowel; revealed 18 June 1936

Soyo.name: Soyombo
Soyo.source_note: created in 1686 by Zanabazar on the model of Lantsa, with Tibetan order and shapes

Sund.name: Sundanese
Sund.source_note: Unicode derives Old Sundanese from Pallawa, Pandey from Kawi; used 14th-18th c.

Sunu.name: Sunuwar
Sunu.source_note: a linear alphabet whose structure is modelled upon the Latin alphabet

Sylo.name: Syloti Nagri
Sylo.source_note: a form of Kaithi; earliest manuscript dated 1549 or 1774, exact origin unknown

Syrc.name: Syriac
Syrc.source_note: the earliest dated Syriac inscription is the Birecik inscription of 6 CE

Tagb.name: Tagbanwa
Tagb.source: Unicode ch.17; Miller, Unicode Technical Note 35
Tagb.source_note: related to Tagalog but may not descend from it; within the range of 17th-c. Philippine handwriting

Takr.name: Takri, Ṭākrī, Ṭāṅkrī
Takr.source_note: from Sharada through Devasesha (14th c.), differentiated in the 16th c.; official in princely states until the mid-20th c.; revival efforts only

Tale.name: Tai Le
Tale.source: Daniels 2012, Journal of Southeast Asian Studies
Tale.source_note: the Tay borrowed heavily from Burmese before the 15th c.; a Ming scroll of 1407

Talu.name: New Tai Lue
Talu.source_note: a simplification of Tai Tham, officially introduced 1955

Taml.name: Tamil
Taml.source_note: a new alphabet for Tamil around the start of the 7th c., a sister of Grantha, not from Vatteluttu

Tang.name: Tangut
Tang.source_note: invented by decree with Chinese writing as conceptual model; no shared characters

Tavt.name: Tai Viet
Tavt.source_note: Tai Dam script a derivative of Sukhothai script, arriving around the 16th c.

Tayo.name: Tai Yo
Tayo.source_note: a common origin with the Tai Dam group; written top to bottom in right-to-left columns; teaching and learning supported by local government and teachers

Telu.name: Telugu
Telu.source_note: Kalamalla inscription of the Renati Cholas, end of the 6th c.

Teng.name: Tengwar
Teng.source_note: the featural Tengwar, developed by Tolkien from Sarati

Tfng.name: Tifinagh (Berber)
Tfng.source: British Museum, 'Written in stone'; Chaker & Hachi 2000
Tfng.source_note: Phoenician/Punic origin has the wider support; indigenous and South Arabian origins argued; first dated text 139/138 BCE (Dougga)

Tglg.name: Tagalog (Baybayin, Alibata)
Tglg.source_note: Kawi, Bugis, Sumatran and Gujarati origins all argued; first verifiably dated text 1593

Thaa.name: Thaana
Thaa.source: Maldives National Centre for Linguistic and Historical Research, 'Scripts of Maldives'
Thaa.source_note: first nine letters from Arabic numerals, next nine from Indic numerals; vowel marks from Arabic; earliest records 1705

Thai.name: Thai
Thai.source_note: Ram Khamhaeng inscription dated 1292, authenticity disputed; Wat Bang Sanuk 1219 also cited

Tibt.name: Tibetan
Tibt.source: van Schaik 2012, in Tibetan manuscript studies
Tibt.source_note: north Indian and Nepalese late Gupta inscriptions the closest models

Tirh.name: Tirhuta
Tirh.source: Pandey, L2/11-175R, after Salomon 1998; Unicode ch.15
Tirh.source_note: derived from Gaudi (proto-Bengali); a sibling of Bengali, not its child; inscriptions 13th c.; still used for religious and literary manuscripts and personal letters

Tnsa.name: Tangsa
Tnsa.source_note: developed since 1990 by Lakhum Mossang; genetically unrelated to existing scripts

Todr.name: Todhri
Todr.source_note: derived from Greek and Roman cursive (Geitler); 18th century, author fl. c.1730-1805

Tols.name: Tolong Siki
Tols.source_note: invented in 1988 by Narayan Oraon, published 1999

Toto.name: Toto
Toto.source_note: an entirely novel set of letters from everyday objects; launched May 2015

Tutg.name: Tulu-Tigalari
Tutg.source_note: evolved from the later Chola Grantha to write Sanskrit; in continuous use for ritual purposes such as birth charts and charms
Tutg.glyph_miss: no Noto face published (tried NotoSansTuluTigalari, NotoSerifTuluTigalari, NotoTuluTigalari)

Ugar.name: Ugaritic
Ugar.source_note: modelled on a linear alphabet of 27 signs; only the wedge medium is Mesopotamian

Vaii.name: Vai
Vaii.source: Unicode ch.19; Tuchscherer & Hair 2002, History in Africa 29
Vaii.source_note: Latin, Arabic and possibly Cherokee influence proposed; none established

Visp.name: Visible Speech
Visp.source_note: symbols built from the vocal organs, not from existing letters

Vith.name: Vithkuqi
Vith.source: Everson, Unicode N5138, quoting Elsie 2017 and von Hahn
Vith.source_note: only single letters recall Greek; glyphs resemble cursive Armenian; no source names a model

Wara.name: Warang Citi (Varang Kshiti)
Wara.source_note: devised by Lako Bodra in the 1950s; full vowel letters

Wcho.name: Wancho
Wcho.source_note: devised 2001-2012 by Banwang Losu; a simple alphabetic script

Wole.name: Woleai
Wole.source_note: one class of signs from Latin letters, the other invented; c.1905-1909

Xpeo.name: Old Persian
Xpeo.source_note: an independent creation in wedge form for Darius's Bisotun inscription, c. 520 BCE

Xsux.name: Cuneiform, Sumero-Akkadian
Xsux.source_note: cuneiform proper from c.2700-2600 BCE (Fara, Abu Salabikh); -2900 is the end of the archaic period

Yezi.name: Yezidi
Yezi.source_note: an original consonantal alphabet; manuscripts perhaps 12th-13th c.; no named ancestor

Yiii.name: Yi
Yiii.source_note: glyphs independent in form; earliest dated object a bronze bell of 1485

Zanb.name: Zanabazar Square (Zanabazarin Dörböljin Useg, Xewtee Dörböljin Bicig, Horizontal Square Script)
Zanb.source_note: based upon Tibetan; date unknown, believed to precede Soyombo (1686)
